page: Microsoft Azure E96ads_v5 is an EADSv5-family virtual machine running on the Microsoft Hyper-V hypervisor. It features 96 dedicated vCPUs mapped to 48 physical cores of an AMD EPYC 7763 processor operating at 3.7 GHz. The system architecture is x86_64, utilizing simultaneous multithreading with two threads per core. Memory capacity is 672.0 GB, providing 7.0 GB of RAM per core. Local storage is bundled, offering 3686 GB of local disk capacity, and the instance is Premium Storage capable. No GPUs are included in this configuration, and it does not come with complimentary public IPv4 addresses.

Benchmark data indicates strong multi-core processing capabilities, with stress-ng multi-core CPU performance ranking in the top tier (top 10%) and a PassMark CPU encryption test also placing in the top tier. The PassMark memory score is in the top tier, supported by a strong (top 25%) memory bandwidth read-only small block speed of 6081.25 GB/sec, though large block read and write memory bandwidths fall into the average (middle 50%) category. Single-core performance is moderate, with Geekbench single-core and stress-ng single-core scores registering in the average and strong categories respectively. Multi-threaded decompression via bzip3 and software compilation with Clang both show strong (top 25%) performance.

Given the high memory-to-vCPU ratio of 7.0 GB per core and the inclusion of 3686 GB of local storage, this instance is configured for memory-intensive workloads and database operations. PassMark database operations and Redis SET operations both achieved strong (top 25%) benchmark results. For machine learning, the server demonstrates strong (top 25%) LLM inference speeds for small models, though performance drops to average for medium and large models due to the lack of dedicated GPU hardware. The high resource density of 96 vCPUs and 672.0 GB of RAM provides qualitative cost efficiency for large-scale relational databases, in-memory caching, and data analytics pipelines that require substantial memory without requiring GPU acceleration.

Large-block memory bandwidth and single-core processing remain in the average tier. Lacking a GPU, it relies on CPU-based execution, showing strong performance in small LLM inference but average speeds on larger models. This configuration is suited for memory-intensive databases, enterprise applications, and large-scale data processing workloads.
